To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

PBDE levels in peregrines increased 3-fold each decade in California, while PCB levels remained constant; the urban pattern of higher proportions of higher brominated congeners was consistent with the diet of urban peregrine prey, and the patterns of PBDEs changed over time in the birds, consistent with metabolic debromoination and accumulation of BDE-47
High levels of polybromodiphenyl ether (PBDE) and polychorinated biphenyl (PCB) contaminants were measured in peregine falcon eggs collected in California, 1986- 2007.

the highest levels of PBDEs were found in peregrines from major California cities, and that the patterns of PBDEs in urban birds were similar to the patterns in the urban prey birds, with a higher proportion of higher-brominated (short half-life) PBDEs than in the coastal birds.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fate of PBDEs in California peregines and the potential for biomagnification of the higher brominated congeners, including the banned BDE-209, in the environment.
environmental contamination and its effects on wildlife.

the fate and transport of PBDEs in the environment, with a particular interest in the metabolic debromination and bioaccumulation of BDE-207 and -209, and the implications of the debrominated PBDE products for wildlife.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(a) BDE-209 is being released from products as an environmental pollutant, (b) BDE-153 is the most persistent of the lower-brominated BDEs, (c) BDE-47 is the least persistent of the lower brominated BDEs.
the peregrine data indicate a significant change over time in the PBDE pattern of peregrines (i.e., a change in relative proportions of the congeners) that was not observed in the PCBs.

(a) BDE-209 is an environmental contaminant; (b) BDE-153 is an environmental contaminatant, but not as widespread as BDE-209; and (c) the lower brominated congeners are environmental contaminants, but are not as widespread or as high in levels as the higher brominated congeners, and are not as persistent in the environment as BDE-153.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the banned PBDEs are not banned, and that the banned BDE-209 is a major environmental contaminant that is being taken up and metabolized in wildlife.

peregrine populations have been exposed to increasing levels of PBDEs in their environment and in their diet, and that the patterns of PBDEs are changing over time in these populations, with higher proportions of BDL-209 (and other higher brominated PBDES) in young birds, and higher proportions of BDEL-153 (and other lower brominated congeners) in older birds.

BDE-47, -99, -100, and -153 were the most abundant and persistent PBDEs in peregrines, with the highest levels of BDE-47 in the Coastal regions and the highest levels of all four of these congeners in the Big Cities.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the higher brominated congeners, particularly BDE-209, are the major contributors to the PBDE body burdens in wildlife, and the lower brominated congeners are secondary contaminants. (C) 2010 Elsevier B.V. All
